# Part 1 — Explore the Dataset

## Background

We use a soil survey transect dataset from **West Virginia** throughout this exercise.
The dataset contains field-collected pedon observations linked to environmental covariates
derived from terrain analysis, remote sensing, and climate surfaces — the standard
input data structure for digital soil mapping (DSM).

**Response variables used in this exercise:**

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `spodint` | Ordered factor | Spodic intensity (0–2) — used for classification |
| `Otot` | Continuous | O horizon thickness (cm) — used for regression and RF |

**Key environmental covariates** include terrain derivatives (DEM, slope, aspect, TWI),
Landsat reflectance bands, NDVI, solar radiation, and mean annual rainfall.


## Load and Map Data

```{r load-data}
# Download the WV transect data from GitHub
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ncss-tech/stats_for_soil_survey/master/data/logistic/wv_transect_editedforR.csv"
download.file(url, "soildata.csv", mode = "wb")
soildata <- read.csv("soildata.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")

# Convert to spatial object for mapping
soildata_sf <- st_as_sf(
  soildata,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs    = 4326
)

# Interactive map of sampling locations
mapview(soildata_sf, zcol = "depth_cm", layer.name = "Soil Depth (cm)")@map
```

```{r write-shapefile, eval=FALSE}
# Optional: write shapefile for use in GIS
write_sf(soildata_sf, dsn = "soildata.shp")
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r eda-structure}
# Reload as flat data frame for modeling
soildata <- read.csv("soildata.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")

soildata$spodint  <- ordered(as.factor(soildata$spodint))
soildata$tipmound <- ordered(as.factor(soildata$tipmound))

str(soildata)
```

```{r eda-plots, fig.height=4}
# Spodic intensity vs solar radiation
p1 <- ggplot(soildata, aes(x = spodint, y = solar)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#5b9bd5", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Spodic Intensity", y = "Solar Radiation",
       title = "Solar Radiation by Spodic Intensity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Spodic intensity vs northwestness (aspect proxy)
p2 <- ggplot(soildata, aes(x = spodint, y = northwestn)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#70ad47", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Spodic Intensity", y = "Northwestness",
       title = "Aspect (Northwestness) by Spodic Intensity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

> **Interpretation:** Solar radiation tends to decrease with higher spodic intensity — 
> cooler, shaded north-facing positions favor the leaching processes that produce 
> spodic horizons. This is the kind of soil-landscape relationship a decision tree 
> will attempt to quantify and formalize.

```{r eda-o-horizon}
# O horizon thickness by soil order
ggplot(soildata, aes(x = Otot)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#8b6914", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ order, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "O Horizon Thickness (cm)", y = "Density",
       title = "O Horizon Distribution by Soil Order") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

# Part 2 — Classification Tree: Predicting Spodic Intensity

## Theory: Gini Impurity and Information Gain

For classification tasks, CART chooses splits that minimize **node impurity** 
rather than RSS. Two common impurity measures:

**Gini Impurity** (CART default):
$$G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$$
where $p_k$ is the class proportion. A pure node ($G = 0$) contains only one class.

**Entropy** (used by C4.5 / information gain):
$$H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2(p_k)$$

*Example with 80% Spodic / 20% Non-Spodic (binary case):*

- Gini: $G = 1 - (0.8^2 + 0.2^2) = 0.32$  
- Entropy: $H = -(0.8 \log_2 0.8 + 0.2 \log_2 0.2) = 0.72$ bits

For an **ordered multi-class** response like `spodint` (levels 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2), 
CART still uses Gini or entropy but now sums across all five class proportions at each node.
The ordered structure is preserved — the tree can learn that intensity level 0 and 0.5 
behave similarly while separating from 1.5 and 2.

| Parameter | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `minsplit` | 20 | minimum observations in a node to attempt a split |
| `minbucket` | `minsplit/3` ≈ 7 | minimum observations allowed in a terminal leaf |
| `cp` | 0.01 | minimum proportional RSS improvement required to accept a split |
| `maxdepth` | 30 | maximum tree depth from root to terminal node |
| `maxcompete` | 4 | number of competitor splits reported per node |
| `xval` | 10 | number of cross-validation folds for CP table |

> **Tip:** For most soil classification tasks, Gini and entropy produce nearly 
> identical trees. Gini is faster (no logarithm). Use entropy when class 
> probabilities matter more than just the predicted class label.

## Data Preparation

```{r classify-prep}
# Fresh read — classification task
soildata <- read.csv("soildata.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")

# Keep spodint as an ordered factor (0 < 0.5 < 1 < 1.5 < 2)
soildata$spodint  <- ordered(as.factor(soildata$spodint))
soildata$tipmound <- ordered(as.factor(soildata$tipmound))

# Class distribution across all 5 intensity levels
table(soildata$spodint)
```

```{r classify-split}
set.seed(42)
# 70/30 split — aligns with 006-treemodels approach
datasplit <- sample(nrow(soildata), nrow(soildata) * 0.7)
train_sp  <- soildata[ datasplit, ]
test_sp   <- soildata[-datasplit, ]

xvars_class <- c(
  "rainfall", "geology", "aachn", "dem10m", "downslpgra", "eastness",
  "greenrefl", "landsatb1", "landsatb2", "landsatb3", "landsatb7",
  "maxc100", "maxent", "minc100", "mirref", "ndvi",
  "northeastn", "northness", "northwestn", "planc100", "proc100",
  "protection", "relpos11", "slp50", "solar", "tanc75"
)
```

## Model 1: Multi-Class spodint

We start by predicting **all five spodic intensity classes** (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2) directly.
This mirrors the original field measurement and preserves the full gradient of spodic expression.

```{r spodint-model1, fig.height=6}
spodintmodel <- rpart(
  spodint ~ rainfall + geology + aachn + dem10m + downslpgra + eastness + greenrefl +
    landsatb1 + landsatb2 + landsatb3 + landsatb7 + maxc100 + maxent + minc100 +
    mirref + ndvi + northeastn + northness + northwestn + planc100 + proc100 +
    protection + relpos11 + slp50 + solar + tanc75,
  data   = train_sp,
  method = "class"
)

# Text summary
# spodintmodel
```

```{r spodint-model1-plot, fig.height=6}
# Misclassification rate at node (incorrect / total in node)
rpart.plot(spodintmodel, extra = 3,
           main = "Spodic Intensity — Multi-Class (extra=3)")

# Adding 100 shows percentage of observations in each node
rpart.plot(spodintmodel, extra = 103,
           main = "Spodic Intensity — Multi-Class (extra=103)")
```

> Notice that terminal nodes display spodic intensity classes 0–2. The tree must learn 
> to separate five classes using the same covariates, making this a harder problem 
> than binary classification.

## Model 2: Binary (Spodic / Non-Spodic)

An alternative framing: collapse the intensity scale into **spodic vs non-spodic**, 
analogous to Nauman et al. (2015). Intensity ≤ 0.5 = non-spodic; ≥ 1 = spodic.
This simplifies the prediction task but loses information about degree of expression.

```{r spodint-model2, fig.height=6}
# Recode spodint into binary response
index  <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)
values <- c("nonspodic", "nonspodic", "spodic", "spodic", "spodic")
soildata$spo_binary  <- as.factor(values[match(soildata$spodint, index)])
train_sp$spo_binary  <- as.factor(values[match(train_sp$spodint, index)])
test_sp$spo_binary   <- as.factor(values[match(test_sp$spodint, index)])

spodintmodel2 <- rpart(
  spo_binary ~ rainfall + geology + aachn + dem10m + downslpgra + eastness + greenrefl +
    landsatb1 + landsatb2 + landsatb3 + landsatb7 + maxc100 + maxent + minc100 +
    mirref + ndvi + northeastn + northness + northwestn + planc100 + proc100 +
    protection + relpos11 + slp50 + solar + tanc75,
  data   = train_sp,
  method = "class", parms = list(split = "gini")
)
spodintmodel3 <- rpart(
  spo_binary ~ rainfall + geology + aachn + dem10m + downslpgra + eastness + greenrefl +
    landsatb1 + landsatb2 + landsatb3 + landsatb7 + maxc100 + maxent + minc100 +
    mirref + ndvi + northeastn + northness + northwestn + planc100 + proc100 +
    protection + relpos11 + slp50 + solar + tanc75,
  data   = train_sp,
  method = "class", parms = list(split = "information")
)
spodintmodel2
spodintmodel3
```

```{r spodint-model2-plot, fig.height=5, fig.width=14}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
rpart.plot(spodintmodel2, extra = 103, box.palette = "GnBu",
           main = "Full Tree: Gini impurity")
rpart.plot(spodintmodel3, extra = 103, box.palette = "OrRd",
           main = "Full Tree: Information (entropy)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The two criteria build different full trees. Check the structure:

```{r gini-vs-entropy-structure}
# Node and split counts for each criterion
gini_leaves <- sum(spodintmodel2$frame$var == "<leaf>")
info_leaves <- sum(spodintmodel3$frame$var == "<leaf>")

cat(sprintf("Gini      — terminal nodes: %d,  total nodes: %d\n",
            gini_leaves, nrow(spodintmodel2$frame)))
cat(sprintf("Entropy   — terminal nodes: %d,  total nodes: %d\n",
            info_leaves, nrow(spodintmodel3$frame)))

# Root and top splits for each
cat("\n--- Gini: top 3 splits ---\n")
print(spodintmodel2$frame[spodintmodel2$frame$var != "<leaf>",
                           c("var", "n", "dev"), drop = FALSE][1:min(3, sum(spodintmodel2$frame$var != "<leaf>")), ])

cat("\n--- Entropy: top 3 splits ---\n")
print(spodintmodel3$frame[spodintmodel3$frame$var != "<leaf>",
                           c("var", "n", "dev"), drop = FALSE][1:min(3, sum(spodintmodel3$frame$var != "<leaf>")), ])
```

```{r gini-vs-entropy-deep, fig.height=4}
# Visualise where the splits diverge: compare paths to all terminal nodes
gini_path <- path.rpart(spodintmodel2, nodes = as.integer(
  row.names(spodintmodel2$frame[spodintmodel2$frame$var == "<leaf>", ])),
  print.it = FALSE)
info_path <- path.rpart(spodintmodel3, nodes = as.integer(
  row.names(spodintmodel3$frame[spodintmodel3$frame$var == "<leaf>", ])),
  print.it = FALSE)

# Summarise: which variables appear in each tree's splits
gini_vars <- unique(as.character(
  spodintmodel2$frame$var[spodintmodel2$frame$var != "<leaf>"]))
info_vars <- unique(as.character(
  spodintmodel3$frame$var[spodintmodel3$frame$var != "<leaf>"]))

cat("Variables used — Gini only:      ", paste(setdiff(gini_vars, info_vars), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Variables used — Entropy only:   ", paste(setdiff(info_vars, gini_vars), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Variables used — both criteria:  ", paste(intersect(gini_vars, info_vars), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

> These divergences are in the **deep nodes** where sample sizes are small and the
> impurity difference between competing splits is tiny. Gini and entropy have
> different curvature near equal class proportions, so they rank marginal splits
> differently — producing different subtrees in the lower branches.

Now prune both with the 1-SE rule:

```{r gini-vs-entropy-pruned, fig.height=5, fig.width=14}
cp_1se_gini <- {
  tbl <- spodintmodel2$cptable
  xe  <- tbl[, "xerror"]; xs <- tbl[, "xstd"]
  mi  <- which.min(xe)
  tbl[min(which(xe <= xe[mi] + xs[mi])), "CP"]
}
cp_1se_info <- {
  tbl <- spodintmodel3$cptable
  xe  <- tbl[, "xerror"]; xs <- tbl[, "xstd"]
  mi  <- which.min(xe)
  tbl[min(which(xe <= xe[mi] + xs[mi])), "CP"]
}

pruned_gini <- prune(spodintmodel2, cp = cp_1se_gini)
pruned_info <- prune(spodintmodel3, cp = cp_1se_info)

cat(sprintf("Pruned Gini    — terminal nodes: %d  (from %d)\n",
            sum(pruned_gini$frame$var == "<leaf>"), gini_leaves))
cat(sprintf("Pruned Entropy — terminal nodes: %d  (from %d)\n",
            sum(pruned_info$frame$var == "<leaf>"), info_leaves))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
rpart.plot(pruned_gini, extra = 103, box.palette = "GnBu",
           main = "Pruned (1-SE): Gini")
rpart.plot(pruned_info, extra = 103, box.palette = "OrRd",
           main = "Pruned (1-SE): Entropy")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r gini-vs-entropy-accuracy}
pred_gini <- predict(pruned_gini, newdata = test_sp, type = "class")
pred_info <- predict(pruned_info, newdata = test_sp, type = "class")

acc_gini <- mean(pred_gini == test_sp$spo_binary)
acc_info <- mean(pred_info == test_sp$spo_binary)

cat(sprintf("Test accuracy — Gini pruned:    %.4f\n", acc_gini))
cat(sprintf("Test accuracy — Entropy pruned: %.4f\n", acc_info))
cat(sprintf("Difference:                     %.4f\n", abs(acc_gini - acc_info)))
```

> After 1-SE pruning, the deep noise-driven branches are removed from both trees,
> leaving only splits with a large, consistent impurity reduction — strong enough
> that Gini and entropy rank them identically. The pruned trees typically share the
> same structure and produce the same (or within rounding identical) test accuracy.

> **Notice that several of the splits changed compared to the multi-class model. 
> Which model do you think will perform better? Why?**

## CP Comparison and Pruning

The `printcp()` function generates the cost-complexity table: CP value, relative 
error, 10-fold cross-validation error (`xerror`), and its standard error (`xstd`). 
Use `plotcp()` to visualise the tradeoff between tree size and CV error.

```{r cp-compare, fig.height=4}
# CP tables for both models
cat("=== Multi-class spodint CP table ===\n")
printcp(spodintmodel)

cat("\n=== Binary spodic/nonspodic CP table ===\n")
printcp(spodintmodel2)
```

```{r plotcp-compare, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotcp(spodintmodel,  main = "Multi-Class spodint")
plotcp(spodintmodel2, main = "Binary spo_binary")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r prune-both, fig.height=4}
# Automated 1-SE rule for both models
cp_1se_fn <- function(model) {
  tbl     <- model$cptable
  xerr    <- tbl[, "xerror"]
  xstd    <- tbl[, "xstd"]
  min_idx <- which.min(xerr)
  thresh  <- xerr[min_idx] + xstd[min_idx]
  tbl[min(which(xerr <= thresh)), "CP"]
}

cp1 <- cp_1se_fn(spodintmodel)
cp2 <- cp_1se_fn(spodintmodel2)
cp3 <- cp_1se_fn(spodintmodel3)

cat(sprintf("1-SE CP — multi-class: %.6f\n", cp1))
cat(sprintf("1-SE CP — binary:      %.6f\n", cp2))
cat(sprintf("1-SE CP — binary:      %.6f\n", cp3))
pruned_mc  <- prune(spodintmodel,  cp = cp1)
pruned_bin1 <- prune(spodintmodel2, cp = cp2)
pruned_bin2 <- prune(spodintmodel3, cp = cp3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
# rpart.plot(pruned_mc,  extra = 3, box.palette = "Greens", main = "Pruned — Multi-Class")
rpart.plot(pruned_bin1, extra = 3, box.palette = "GnBu",   main = "Pruned — Binary")
rpart.plot(pruned_bin2, extra = 3, box.palette = "GnBu",   main = "Pruned — Binary")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```


## Confusion Matrix Comparison

Split-sample validation using the held-out 30% test set:

```{r class-accuracy}
# Multi-class predictions
pred_mc  <- predict(pruned_mc,  newdata = test_sp, type = "class")
cm_mc    <- confusionMatrix(pred_mc, test_sp$spodint, mode = "everything")

# Binary predictions
pred_bin <- predict(pruned_bin1, newdata = test_sp, type = "class")
cm_bin   <- confusionMatrix(pred_bin, test_sp$spo_binary, mode = "everything")

# Summary
results_tbl <- data.frame(
  Model    = c("Multi-Class (5 levels)", "Binary (spodic/nonspodic)"),
  Accuracy = round(c(cm_mc$overall["Accuracy"],  cm_bin$overall["Accuracy"]), 4),
  Kappa    = round(c(cm_mc$overall["Kappa"],     cm_bin$overall["Kappa"]),    4)
)
print(results_tbl)
```

```{r confusion-matrix-detail}
cat("--- Multi-Class Confusion Matrix (rows=observed, cols=predicted) ---\n")
print(cm_mc$table)

cat("\n--- Binary Confusion Matrix ---\n")
print(cm_bin$table)
```

> **Why does the binary model outperform the multi-class model?**  
> The multi-class tree must separate five classes simultaneously with the same 
> covariates. The rarest intermediate classes (0.5, 1.5) are often misclassified 
> because the training signal is weak. Collapsing to binary removes this ambiguity — 
> the decision boundary between spodic and non-spodic is more environmentally 
> consistent than the boundaries between adjacent intensity levels.

> **Questions:**  
> 1. What was the misclassification rate for each model (root node error × xerror × 100)?  
> 2. Which intensity levels are most commonly confused in the multi-class model? Does this make pedological sense?  
> 3. What are the practical implications of misclassifying a spodic site as non-spodic in a soil survey context?  
> 4. Consider treating `spodint` as numeric (0–2) and building a regression tree. What would a leaf mean of 1.0 tell you about the observations in that node?

# Part 3 — Regression Tree: Predicting O Horizon Thickness

## Theory: How CART Splits

A **regression tree** recursively partitions the feature space into rectangular
regions based on binary splits. At each node, CART evaluates every candidate
split $(j, t)$ — feature $j$ at threshold $t$ — and selects the one that
maximally reduces the **Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)**:

$$\Delta RSS = RSS_{\text{parent}} - \left[ RSS_{\text{left}} + RSS_{\text{right}} \right]$$

Within each leaf, the prediction is the mean of all training samples:
$$\hat{y}_{\text{leaf}} = \frac{1}{N_{\text{leaf}}} \sum_{i \in \text{leaf}} y_i$$

This greedy, top-down algorithm is implemented in R as `rpart()` with `method = "anova"`.

## Build and Inspect Tree

```{r split-data}
set.seed(42)
idx <- createDataPartition(soildata$Otot, p = 0.70, list = FALSE)
cal <- soildata[ idx, ]
val <- soildata[-idx, ]

cat("Calibration samples:", nrow(cal), "\n")
cat("Validation samples: ", nrow(val), "\n")
```

```{r build-regression-tree}
# Define covariate names (reused throughout exercise)
xvars_terrain <- c(
  "rainfall", "dem10m", "downslpgra", "eastness", "greenrefl",
  "landsatb1", "landsatb2", "landsatb3", "landsatb7",
  "maxc100", "maxent", "minc100", "mirref", "ndvi",
  "northeastn", "northness", "northwestn", "planc100",
  "proc100", "protection", "relpos11", "slp50", "solar", "tanc75"
)

tree_full <- rpart(
  formula = as.formula(paste("Otot ~", paste(xvars_terrain, collapse = " + "))),
  data    = cal,
  method  = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 10, minbucket = 5)
)

print(tree_full)
```

```{r plot-full-tree, fig.height=6}
rpart.plot(tree_full,
           type = 4, extra = 101, box.palette = "RdYlGn",
           main = "Full Tree: Otot (cm)")
```

> **How to read this tree:**  
> - **Top of node:** Split condition. Samples satisfying the rule go left; others right.  
> - **Middle:** Predicted O horizon thickness (mean of training samples at this node).  
> - **Bottom:** Percentage of training samples at this node.

## Pruning with Cost-Complexity

Allowing a tree to grow until every leaf contains a single sample produces 
**zero training error but extreme overfitting** — the model has memorized noise
rather than learning relationships. 

**Cost-complexity pruning** penalizes tree size by a complexity parameter $\alpha$ (`cp` in R):

$$R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha \times |T|$$

where $R(T)$ is training error and $|T|$ is the number of leaf nodes. 
As $\alpha$ increases, the optimal tree shrinks. Cross-validation selects 
the best $\alpha$.

```{r cp-diagnostic, fig.height=4}
# Examine the complexity parameter table
printcp(tree_full)

# Plot CV error vs tree size
plotcp(tree_full)
```

The **1-SE rule** selects the *smallest* tree whose CV error is within one standard
error of the minimum — preferring interpretability over minimal CV error:

```{r prune-1se}
# Extract CP table components
cp_tbl  <- tree_full$cptable
xerr    <- cp_tbl[, "xerror"]
xstd    <- cp_tbl[, "xstd"]

# Minimum CV error and its location
min_idx <- which.min(xerr)
thresh  <- xerr[min_idx] + xstd[min_idx]

# 1-SE rule: largest CP (simplest tree) still within 1 SE of the minimum
cp_1se  <- cp_tbl[min(which(xerr <= thresh)), "CP"]
cat(sprintf("Minimum-error CP: %.5f\n", cp_tbl[min_idx, "CP"]))
cat(sprintf("1-SE rule CP:     %.5f\n", cp_1se))
```

```{r prune-tree, fig.height=5}
tree_pruned <- prune(tree_full, cp = cp_1se)

rpart.plot(tree_pruned,
           type = 4, extra = 101, box.palette = "RdYlGn",
           main = "Pruned Tree: Otot (cm)")
```

## Model Accuracy Comparison

```{r regression-accuracy}
# Predict on validation set
pred_full   <- predict(tree_full,   newdata = val)
pred_pruned <- predict(tree_pruned, newdata = val)

# RMSE on original Otot scale
rmse_full   <- RMSE(pred = pred_full,   obs = val$Otot)
rmse_pruned <- RMSE(pred = pred_pruned, obs = val$Otot)

rpart_results <- data.frame(
  Model  = c("rpart full", "rpart pruned (1-SE)"),
  RMSE   = round(c(rmse_full, rmse_pruned), 3),
  Leaves = c(sum(tree_full$frame$var == "<leaf>"),
             sum(tree_pruned$frame$var == "<leaf>"))
)
print(rpart_results)
```

```{r rpart-residuals, fig.height=4}
plot(val$Otot, pred_pruned,
     xlab = "Observed Otot (cm)", ylab = "Predicted (cm)",
     main = "rpart pruned: Observed vs Predicted", col = "#8b6914", pch = 16)
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

> **Key insight:** The pruned tree avoids fitting noise despite having far fewer nodes (bias-variance tradeoff).

> **Questions:**  
> 1. What was the root split variable? Does it make pedological sense for O horizon thickness?  
> 2. How much did pruning reduce the number of leaves compared to the full tree?  
> 3. Does the pruned tree RMSE indicate a useful model for field applications?

# Part 4 — Random Forest: O Horizon Thickness

## Theory: Why Ensembles Work

A single decision tree has **high variance** — small changes in training data 
produce very different trees. The core idea of **bagging** (Breiman, 1996) is 
that averaging many high-variance models cancels out their individual noise:

$$\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x)$$

For $B$ trees each with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$:

$$\text{Var}\!\left(\hat{f}_{\text{RF}}\right) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{(1-\rho)\,\sigma^2}{B}$$

**Random Forest's key innovation** (Breiman, 2001): at each split, only a random 
subset of `mtry` features is considered. This **decorrelates** the trees, reducing 
$\rho$ and shrinking the irreducible first term. As $B \to \infty$, 
$\text{Var} \to \rho\sigma^2$.

## Build RF: O Horizon Thickness

We continue with the WV soildata to build a Random Forest regression for total 
O horizon thickness (`Otot`) — the same response variable used in Part 2's 
regression tree — so we can directly compare single-tree vs ensemble performance.

```{r rf-otot}
# Fresh load — ensure clean state
soildata <- read.csv("soildata.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
soildata$spodint  <- ordered(as.factor(soildata$spodint))
soildata$tipmound <- ordered(as.factor(soildata$tipmound))

set.seed(42)
rf_otot <- randomForest(
  Otot ~ rainfall + geology + aachn + dem10m + downslpgra + eastness + greenrefl +
    landsatb1 + landsatb2 + landsatb3 + landsatb7 + maxc100 + maxent + minc100 +
    mirref + ndvi + northeastn + northness + northwestn + planc100 + proc100 +
    protection + relpos11 + slp50 + solar + tanc75,
  data       = soildata,
  importance = TRUE,
  ntree      = 1000,
  mtry       = 10
)

# Statistical summary — % variance explained and MSE
print(rf_otot)
```

```{r rf-otot-convergence, fig.height=4}
# OOB error vs number of trees — use this to tune ntree
plot(rf_otot,
     main = "OOB Error vs Number of Trees (Otot)",
     col  = "#2c5f2e")
```

> The curve should flatten well before 1000 trees. If it is still declining, 
> increase `ntree`. **How does the % variance explained compare to the rpart 
> regression tree from Part 2?**



```{r}
library(caret)
library(ranger)

# ── Covariates ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
predictors <- c(
  "rainfall",   "geology",    "aachn",      "dem10m",     "downslpgra",
  "eastness",   "greenrefl",  "landsatb1",  "landsatb2",  "landsatb3",
  "landsatb7",  "maxc100",    "maxent",     "minc100",    "mirref",
  "ndvi",       "northeastn", "northness",  "northwestn", "planc100",
  "proc100",    "protection", "relpos11",   "slp50",      "solar",
  "tanc75"
)

# ── Tuning grid ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
tuning_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry          = c(5, 8, 10, 13),
  splitrule     = c("variance", "extratrees"),
  min.node.size = c(3, 5, 10, 15, 20)
)

# ── Cross-validation control ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
ctrl <- trainControl(
  method          = "cv",
  number          = 10,
  savePredictions = "final"
)

# ── Train ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rf_tuned <- train(
  x         = soildata[, predictors],
  y         = soildata$Otot,
  method    = "ranger",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = tuning_grid,
  num.trees = 500,
  metric    = "RMSE"
)

# ── Results ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rf_tuned$bestTune
rf_tuned$results

# RMSE surface plot
ggplot(rf_tuned$results,
       aes(x      = min.node.size,
           y      = RMSE,
           colour = factor(mtry),
           group  = factor(mtry))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title  = "RF Tuning — O Horizon Thickness",
       x      = "min.node.size",
       y      = "CV RMSE  (cm)",
       colour = "mtry") +
  theme_minimal()

# ── Refit final model with best parameters ────────────────────────────────────
rf_final <- ranger(
  formula       = Otot ~ .,
  data          = soildata[, c(predictors, "Otot")],
  num.trees     = 500,
  mtry          = rf_tuned$bestTune$mtry,
  min.node.size = rf_tuned$bestTune$min.node.size,
  importance    = "permutation"
)

# ── Diagnostics ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
sqrt(rf_final$prediction.error)          # OOB RMSE

sort(importance(rf_final), decreasing = TRUE)   # variable importance ranked

# ── Plot Variable Importance ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
library(vip)
# Bar chart — works directly with ranger objects
vip(rf_final, num_features = 20,
    aesthetics = list(fill = "#2c5f2e", width = 0.7)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Permutation Importance — O Horizon Thickness")
```

## Effect of Outlier Removal

The `Otot` distribution has a strongly influential outlier — the single 
Histosol observation with very thick O horizons. Let's examine its effect:

```{r rf-otot-hist, fig.height=4}
hist(soildata$Otot, breaks = 20,
     main = "O Horizon Thickness Distribution",
     xlab = "Otot (cm)", col = "#8b6914")
```

```{r rf-otot2}
# Remove the Histosol observation
soildata_nohist <- droplevels(subset(soildata, order != "histosol"))
cat(sprintf("Observations removed: %d\n",
            nrow(soildata) - nrow(soildata_nohist)))

set.seed(42)
rf_otot2 <- randomForest(
  Otot ~ rainfall + geology + aachn + dem10m + downslpgra + eastness + greenrefl +
    landsatb1 + landsatb2 + landsatb3 + landsatb7 + maxc100 + maxent + minc100 +
    mirref + ndvi + northeastn + northness + northwestn + planc100 + proc100 +
    protection + relpos11 + slp50 + solar + tanc75,

  importance = TRUE,
  ntree      = 1000,
  mtry       = 9
)

# Compare both models side by side
cat("--- With Histosol ---\n")
cat(sprintf("  %% Var explained: %.1f%%\n", rf_otot$rsq[1000] * 100))
cat(sprintf("  MSE (OOB):       %.3f\n",    rf_otot$mse[1000]))
cat(sprintf("  RMSE (OOB):      %.3f cm\n", sqrt(rf_otot$mse[1000])))

cat("\n--- Without Histosol ---\n")
cat(sprintf("  %% Var explained: %.1f%%\n", rf_otot2$rsq[1000] * 100))
cat(sprintf("  MSE (OOB):       %.3f\n",    rf_otot2$mse[1000]))
cat(sprintf("  RMSE (OOB):      %.3f cm\n", sqrt(rf_otot2$mse[1000])))
```

```{r}
# ── Train ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rf_tuned <- train(
  x         = soildata_nohist[, predictors],
  y         = soildata_nohist$Otot,
  method    = "ranger",
  trControl = ctrl,

# ── Results ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rf_tuned$bestTune
rf_tuned$results

# RMSE surface plot
ggplot(rf_tuned$results,
       aes(x      = min.node.size,
           y      = RMSE,
           colour = factor(mtry),
           group  = factor(mtry))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +

       x      = "min.node.size",

# ── Refit final model with best parameters ────────────────────────────────────
```

## Model Comparison: rpart vs RF

To compare rpart and Random Forest fairly, **both models must be trained on the
same data and evaluated on the same held-out set**.

| Evaluation method | What it measures | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Split-sample** (val set) | Error on truly unseen data from a fixed 30% holdout | Directly comparable across model types |
| **OOB** | Bootstrap leave-one-out estimate from the full training set | RF-specific; model saw all data; not comparable to val-set RMSE |

Both models are trained on `cal_nohist` (70%, Histosol removed) and evaluated on
`val`. Removing the Histosol from *both* training sets ensures neither model's
performance is driven by a single extreme outlier. `rf_final` (full-data) is
preserved for downstream DSM use.

> **Note on the 1-SE rule and outliers:** The Histosol is the dominant source of
> variance in `Otot`. Removing it from `cal` can cause the 1-SE rule to choose a
> stump (no splits) because even the smallest tree is within one standard error of
> the minimum CV error — the signal is too weak to justify any split with confidence.
> When this happens the code falls back to the minimum-error CP, which keeps the
> splits the data *can* support. This is itself a teaching point: the 1-SE rule
> is conservative, and outliers can inflate apparent signal.

```{r rf-model-comparison}
# ── Shared training set: cal minus Histosol ───────────────────────────────────
cal_nohist <- droplevels(subset(cal, order != "histosol"))

# ── Rebuild rpart on cal_nohist — same formula and 1-SE rule ─────────────────
tree_full_nh <- rpart(
  formula = as.formula(paste("Otot ~", paste(xvars_terrain, collapse = " + "))),
  data    = cal_nohist,
  method  = "anova",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 10, minbucket = 5)
)
cp_tbl_nh <- tree_full_nh$cptable
xerr_nh   <- cp_tbl_nh[, "xerror"]
xstd_nh   <- cp_tbl_nh[, "xstd"]
min_nh    <- which.min(xerr_nh)
thresh_nh <- xerr_nh[min_nh] + xstd_nh[min_nh]

# 1-SE CP — use min-error CP as fallback if 1-SE collapses to a stump
cp_1se_nh <- cp_tbl_nh[min(which(xerr_nh <= thresh_nh)), "CP"]
tree_pruned_nh <- prune(tree_full_nh, cp = cp_1se_nh)
n_leaves_nh    <- sum(tree_pruned_nh$frame$var == "<leaf>")

if (n_leaves_nh == 1) {
  # 1-SE collapsed to stump — removing the Histosol eliminated the dominant
  # variance source; fall back to the minimum-error CP to keep usable splits
  message("1-SE rule produced a stump on cal_nohist; falling back to min-error CP.")
  cp_1se_nh      <- cp_tbl_nh[min_nh, "CP"]
  tree_pruned_nh <- prune(tree_full_nh, cp = cp_1se_nh)
  n_leaves_nh    <- sum(tree_pruned_nh$frame$var == "<leaf>")
  rpart_label    <- "rpart pruned (min-error CP, fallback) [*]"
} else {
  rpart_label    <- "rpart pruned (1-SE CP) [*]"
}

pred_rpart_nh <- predict(tree_pruned_nh, newdata = val)
rmse_rpart_nh <- RMSE(pred = pred_rpart_nh, obs = val$Otot)
r2_rpart_nh   <- cor(pred_rpart_nh, val$Otot)^2

cat(sprintf("rpart (cal_nohist) — leaves: %d  CP used: %.5f\n",
            n_leaves_nh, cp_1se_nh))

# ── RF on cal_nohist — best hyperparameters from earlier tuning ───────────────
set.seed(42)
rf_val_compare <- ranger(
  formula       = Otot ~ .,
  data          = cal_nohist[, c(predictors, "Otot")],
  num.trees     = 500,
  mtry          = rf_tuned$bestTune$mtry,
  min.node.size = rf_tuned$bestTune$min.node.size,
  importance    = "none"
)

pred_rf_val <- predict(rf_val_compare, data = val)$predictions
rmse_rf_val <- RMSE(pred = pred_rf_val, obs = val$Otot)
r2_rf_val   <- cor(pred_rf_val, val$Otot)^2

# ── OOB metrics from full-data RF — for reference only ───────────────────────
rmse_rf_oob <- sqrt(rf_otot2$mse[1000])
r2_rf_oob   <- rf_otot2$rsq[1000]

# ── Comparison table ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
comparison <- data.frame(
  Model        = c(
    rpart_label,
    "Random Forest - val set [*]",
    "Random Forest - OOB [ref]"
  ),
  Trained_on   = c(
    "cal_nohist 70%",
    "cal_nohist 70%",
    "all data (no Histosol)"
  ),
  Evaluated_on = c(
    "val 30%",
    "val 30%",
    "OOB bootstrap"
  ),
  RMSE_cm = round(c(rmse_rpart_nh, rmse_rf_val, rmse_rf_oob), 3),
  R2      = round(c(r2_rpart_nh,   r2_rf_val,   r2_rf_oob),   3)
)
print(comparison)

cat("\n[*]  Direct head-to-head: identical training data (cal_nohist), identical val set.\n")
cat("[ref] OOB reference only: RF trained on full data, not comparable to val-set rows.\n")
```

```{r rf-val-scatter, fig.height=4}
# Observed vs predicted on the same val set — matched training data
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))  # tighten top margin

plot(val$Otot, pred_rpart_nh,
     xlab = "Observed (cm)", ylab = "Predicted (cm)",
     col = "#8b6914", pch = 16)
title(main = bquote(atop("rpart pruned",
                         RMSE == .(round(rmse_rpart_nh, 2)) ~~ R^2 == .(round(r2_rpart_nh, 2)))))
abline(0, 1, col = "red")

plot(val$Otot, pred_rf_val,
     xlab = "Observed (cm)", ylab = "Predicted (cm)",
     col = "#2c5f2e", pch = 16)
title(main = bquote(atop("Random Forest",
                         RMSE == .(round(rmse_rf_val, 2)) ~~ R^2 == .(round(r2_rf_val, 2)))))
abline(0, 1, col = "red")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> **Interpretation:**  
> Rows 1 and 2 are a true head-to-head comparison — identical training set
> (`cal_nohist`), identical evaluation set (`val`). Any difference in RMSE and R²
> is due solely to the algorithm, not data leakage or sample composition. The OOB
> row uses the full dataset for training; it cannot be fairly compared to the
> val-set rows even though OOB is theoretically unbiased on its own training set.
>
> The observed vs predicted plots reveal *why* rpart achieves competitive RMSE
> despite being the simpler model. The pruned tree reduced to a single split on
> `landsatb7`, producing exactly **two possible predictions** — every observation
> is assigned either the low-group mean (~4.5 cm) or the high-group mean (~9.5 cm).
> The two horizontal bands in the left panel make this explicit. An RMSE of 4.91 cm
> is being achieved by a model that cannot distinguish a 3 cm O horizon from a
> 6 cm one if they fall on the same side of the landsatb7 threshold. This is not
> evidence that rpart is a better model — it is evidence that the dominant signal
> in a 177-observation training set is a single SWIR-reflectance threshold
> separating moist forested sites (thick O) from drier sites (thin O), and that
> the 1-SE pruning rule correctly identifies this as the only split justified by
> the data.
>
> Random Forest (right panel) produces a continuous prediction surface and shows
> the expected positive trend along the 1:1 line, but pays an accuracy penalty
> on this small validation set (73 observations) because it is attempting to
> learn a complex multivariate surface from limited signal. The 0.19 cm RMSE
> difference between the two models is well within the sampling uncertainty of
> a 73-sample validation set and should not be interpreted as a meaningful
> performance gap. With substantially more training data (>1,000 observations),
> RF would be expected to pull ahead as the complex surface it learns becomes
> better supported by the data.

> **Questions:**  
> 1. Compare rows 1 and 2 (same training data, same val set). How much does RF reduce RMSE over rpart?  
> 2. Does removing the Histosol change which model appears superior? What does this tell you about outlier sensitivity?  
> 3. Why is the OOB RMSE (row 3) not a fair comparison to rows 1–2, even though OOB is considered unbiased?  
> 4. What does R² add over RMSE for communicating model quality?

## Variable Importance

For regression RF, two importance metrics are reported:  
- **%IncMSE**: average increase in OOB MSE when the variable is permuted. Larger = more important.  
- **IncNodePurity**: total reduction in RSS across all splits on this variable, summed across all trees. Faster to compute but biased toward continuous/high-cardinality variables.

```{r rf-importance, fig.height=6}
varImpPlot(rf_otot2,
           main = "Variable Importance — O Horizon Thickness (Histosol removed)",
           col  = "#2c5f2e")
```

```{r rf-importance-table}
# Sorted tabular importance — useful for reporting
randomForest::importance(rf_otot2) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  arrange(desc(`%IncMSE`))
```


> **Questions:**  
> 1. Did removing the Histosol outlier improve % variance explained?  
> 2. What is the OOB error (MSE and % variance explained)? How does this compare with the rpart regression tree from Part 2?  
> 3. Which variable had the highest %IncMSE? What soil-forming factor does this represent?  
> 4. Do %IncMSE and IncNodePurity agree on the ranking of top predictors? If not, why might they differ?

# Part 5 — Feature Selection with Boruta

## Theory: Why Feature Selection Matters

With many environmental covariates available (terrain + spectral + climate), 
some predictors are noise. Including irrelevant features:

- Increases computation time
- Can reduce model accuracy via the "curse of dimensionality"
- Complicates interpretation

**Boruta** is a wrapper around Random Forest that identifies relevant features
by comparing each predictor's importance against the importance of shuffled
"shadow" copies of itself. Features that consistently outperform their shadow 
are confirmed as important.

## Run Boruta

```{r boruta, cache=TRUE, fig.height=5}
# Fresh load for O horizon thickness prediction
soildata <- read.csv("soildata.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
yvar  <- "Otot"
xvars_bor <- c(
  "rainfall", "geology", "aachn", "dem10m", "downslpgra", "eastness",
  "greenrefl", "landsatb1", "landsatb2", "landsatb3", "landsatb7",
  "maxc100", "maxent", "minc100", "mirref", "ndvi",
  "northeastn", "northness", "northwestn", "planc100", "proc100",
  "protection", "relpos11", "slp50", "solar", "tanc75"
)

set.seed(42)
fs_bor <- Boruta(
  y       = soildata[[yvar]],
  x       = soildata[, xvars_bor],
  maxRuns = 50,
  doTrace = 1
)

# Variable importance plot (green = confirmed, yellow = tentative, red = rejected)
plot(fs_bor,
     xlab = "", las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7,
     main = "Boruta Feature Selection: O Horizon Thickness")
```

```{r boruta-results}
# Confirmed important features
vars_confirmed <- getSelectedAttributes(fs_bor)
cat("Confirmed important features:\n")
print(vars_confirmed)

cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d features confirmed important.\n",
            length(vars_confirmed), length(xvars_bor)))

# Detailed attribute statistics
attrib_stats <- attStats(fs_bor)
attrib_stats[order(-attrib_stats$meanImp), c("meanImp", "decision")]
```

# Part 6 — Cross-Validation with caret and ranger

## Theory: Why Cross-Validate?

The primary purpose of CV here is **hyperparameter tuning**: `caret` fits ranger
repeatedly across a grid of `mtry`, `min.node.size`, and `splitrule` values,
selecting the combination with the best average held-out RMSE across 10 folds.
CV also generalizes to any model type, making RF directly comparable to rpart or
other algorithms on the same folds.


## 10-Fold CV Without Feature Selection

```{r cv-full, cache=TRUE}
tc <- trainControl(
  method       = "cv",
  number       = 10,
  returnResamp = "all",
  savePredictions = TRUE,
  verboseIter  = FALSE
)

set.seed(42)
dep_tr_full <- train(
  y          = soildata[[yvar]],
  x          = soildata[, xvars_bor],
  method     = "ranger",
  importance = "permutation",
  trControl  = tc
)

print(dep_tr_full)
```

## 10-Fold CV With Boruta Features

```{r cv-boruta, cache=TRUE, dependson="boruta"}
set.seed(42)
dep_tr_bor <- train(
  y          = soildata[[yvar]],
  x          = soildata[, vars_confirmed],
  method     = "ranger",
  importance = "permutation",
  trControl  = tc
)

print(dep_tr_bor)
```

## Compare Results

```{r cv-compare}
# Extract metrics at the selected (best) hyperparameter combination only.
# $results has one row per hyperparameter combo with metrics already averaged
# across all 10 folds — this is NOT cherry-picking across folds.
best_full <- merge(dep_tr_full$bestTune, dep_tr_full$results)
best_bor  <- merge(dep_tr_bor$bestTune,  dep_tr_bor$results)

cv_compare <- data.frame(
  Model = c("All features", "Boruta-selected"),
  RMSE  = round(c(best_full$RMSE,      best_bor$RMSE),      4),
  Rsq   = round(c(best_full$Rsquared,  best_bor$Rsquared),  4),
  MAE   = round(c(best_full$MAE,       best_bor$MAE),       4)
)
print(cv_compare)
```

```{r cv-importance, fig.height=4}
# Variable importance comparison
p_full <- vip::vip(dep_tr_full, num_features = 15,
                   aesthetics = list(fill = "#5b9bd5", width = 0.6)) +
  ggtitle("All Features") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_bor  <- vip::vip(dep_tr_bor,  num_features = 15,
                   aesthetics = list(fill = "#70ad47", width = 0.6)) +
  ggtitle("Boruta-Selected") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_full, p_bor, ncol = 2)
```

> **Application:** Permutation importance provides a data-driven 
> quantification of soil forming factors. If precipitation (`rainfall`) 
> dominates, your model confirms climate-controlled SOC dynamics in this MLRA.
> Document the top-ranked covariates in your MLRA correlation documents as 
> quantitative support for your conceptual soil-landscape model.

> **Questions:**  
> 1. Did feature selection (Boruta) improve or worsen CV RMSE?  
> 2. Which predictor has the highest permutation importance?  
> 3. How does this top predictor relate to the soil-forming factors for O horizon development in WV?

# Part 7 — Partial Dependence Plots

## Theory: What PDPs Show

A **Partial Dependence Plot (PDP)** marginalizes the model's predictions over
all other features to show the average effect of a single predictor:

$$\hat{f}_{x_j}(x_j) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \hat{f}(x_j, \mathbf{x}_{-j,i})$$

Unlike variable importance (which ranks features), PDPs show the *shape* of 
the relationship — whether it is linear, threshold-driven, or non-monotonic.
This is especially useful for communicating soil-landscape relationships to field
scientists.

## Fit Final Model and Plot

```{r pdp-model}
# Refit using CV-tuned hyperparameters from dep_tr_bor (Part 6)
# dep_tr_bor searched mtry, min.node.size, and splitrule via 10-fold CV —
# hardcoding heuristics here would give worse OOB R² than the CV result.
cat("Best hyperparameters from CV (dep_tr_bor):\n")
print(dep_tr_bor$bestTune)

# Guard: bestTune$mtry must not exceed the number of confirmed features.
# A stale cv-boruta cache (trained on a larger feature set) can produce an
# mtry value that is valid for the cached run but too large here.
mtry_final <- min(dep_tr_bor$bestTune$mtry, length(vars_confirmed))
if (mtry_final != dep_tr_bor$bestTune$mtry)
  warning("bestTune$mtry clamped to ", mtry_final,
          " — re-knit with cache cleared to resolve cache inconsistency.")

set.seed(42)
rf_final <- ranger(
  formula       = as.formula(paste(yvar, "~", paste(vars_confirmed, collapse = " + "))),
  data          = soildata[, c(yvar, vars_confirmed)],
  num.trees     = 500,
  mtry          = mtry_final,
  min.node.size = dep_tr_bor$bestTune$min.node.size,
  splitrule     = dep_tr_bor$bestTune$splitrule,
  importance    = "permutation"
)

cat(sprintf("OOB R2:   %.4f\n", rf_final$r.squared))
cat(sprintf("OOB RMSE: %.4f cm\n", sqrt(rf_final$prediction.error)))
```

```{r}
# ── OOB residual diagnostics  ─────────────────────────────
oob_preds  <- rf_final$predictions          # OOB predictions in cm
resid_oob  <- soildata[[yvar]] - oob_preds

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(oob_preds, resid_oob,
     xlab = "OOB Predicted (cm)", ylab = "Residual (cm)",
     main = "OOB Residuals vs Fitted", pch = 16, col = "#2c5f2e")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)
qqnorm(resid_oob, main = "Q-Q Plot: OOB Residuals")
qqline(resid_oob, col = "red")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

oob_rmse <- sqrt(mean(resid_oob^2))
oob_r2   <- 1 - sum(resid_oob^2) / sum((soildata[[yvar]] - mean(soildata[[yvar]]))^2)
cat("OOB RMSE (cm):", round(oob_rmse, 2), "\n")
cat("OOB R\u00b2:      ", round(oob_r2, 3), "\n")

```


```{r pdp-plots, fig.height=4}
# Top 2 predictors from importance
top_vars <- names(sort(rf_final$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
cat("Top predictors:", paste(top_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")

# PDP for top two predictors
pdp1 <- pdp::partial(rf_final, pred.var = top_vars[1],
                     plot = FALSE, grid.resolution = 30)
pdp2 <- pdp::partial(rf_final, pred.var = top_vars[2],
                     plot = FALSE, grid.resolution = 30)


ggplot(pdp1, aes_string(x = top_vars[1], y = "yhat")) +
  geom_line(color = "#2c5f2e", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_rug(data = soildata, aes_string(x = top_vars[1], y = NULL),
           sides = "b", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = top_vars[1], y = "Partial Dependence (O Horizon, cm)",
       title = paste("Partial Dependence:", top_vars[1])) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot(pdp2, aes_string(x = top_vars[2], y = "yhat")) +
  geom_line(color = "#2c5f2e", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_rug(data = soildata, aes_string(x = top_vars[2], y = NULL),
           sides = "b", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = top_vars[2], y = "Partial Dependence (O Horizon, cm)",
       title = paste("Partial Dependence:", top_vars[2])) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r pdp-2way, fig.height=5}
pd_2way <- pdp::partial(
  rf_final,
  pred.var        = top_vars[1:2],
  plot            = FALSE,
  grid.resolution = 20
)

ggplot(pd_2way, aes_string(x = top_vars[1], y = top_vars[2], fill = "yhat")) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "O Horizon (cm)", option = "D") +
  labs(title = "2-Way Partial Dependence", x = top_vars[1], y = top_vars[2]) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

> 1. What is the shape of the top predictor's partial dependence — linear, threshold, or non-monotonic? What soil-forming factor does this suggest?  
> 2. In the 2-way plot, do the two predictors interact (non-parallel isolines) or act independently (parallel bands)?  
> 3. At what value of the top predictor does O horizon thickness increase most steeply? Does this correspond to a known ecological or pedological threshold in WV?

# Part 8 — Model Diagnostics

## Observed vs. Predicted

```{r diagnostics-pred}
# Generate training predictions
soildata$pred_Otot <- predict(rf_final, data = soildata)$predictions
soildata$resid     <- soildata$Otot - soildata$pred_Otot

# 1:1 plot
ggplot(soildata, aes(x = pred_Otot, y = Otot)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#2c5f2e") +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e07b54", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Predicted O Horizon (cm)",
       y = "Observed O Horizon (cm)",
       title = "Observed vs. Predicted (Training Data)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

> **Note:** Training-data 1:1 plots are optimistic for Random Forest due to OOB 
> aggregation. Always evaluate on a held-out validation set or use CV metrics.

## Residual Plots

```{r diagnostics-resid, fig.height=8}
p_res1 <- ggplot(soildata, aes(x = pred_Otot, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#5b9bd5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "#e07b54") +
  labs(x = "Predicted", y = "Residual",
       title = "Residuals vs. Fitted") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_res2 <- ggplot(soildata, aes(x = pred_Otot, y = sqrt(abs(resid)))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#5b9bd5") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "#e07b54") +
  labs(x = "Predicted", y = "√|Residual|",
       title = "Scale-Location (Homoscedasticity Check)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_res3 <- ggplot(soildata, aes(sample = resid)) +
  geom_qq(alpha = 0.5, color = "#5b9bd5") +
  geom_qq_line(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_res1, p_res2, p_res3, ncol = 2)
```

> **Interpreting diagnostics:**  
> - **Residuals vs Fitted:** Should show random scatter around zero. Systematic patterns indicate model misfit.  
> - **Scale-Location:** A flat line indicates homoscedasticity (equal variance). Increasing spread suggests heteroscedasticity.  
> - **Q-Q Plot:** Points should follow the reference line. Deviations in the tails indicate non-normal residuals, which can affect prediction intervals.

# Part 9 — SHAP Analysis

## Theory: Why SHAP?

Permutation importance and PDPs answer *which* variables matter and their *average* effect.
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations, Lundberg & Lee 2017) goes further — it attributes
each prediction to individual feature contributions for **every observation**, not just
on average across the dataset.

**The SHAP decomposition:**
$$\hat{f}(x_i) = \phi_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{ij}$$

where $\phi_0$ is the global baseline (mean prediction) and $\phi_{ij}$ is the contribution
of feature $j$ to observation $i$'s prediction. These values are derived from cooperative
game theory: each feature's contribution is its average marginal contribution across all
possible orderings of features entering the model.

**Why SHAP matters for DSM:**

| Tool | What it shows | Limitation |
|------|--------------|-----------|
| Permutation VIP | Global ranking only | No per-observation detail |
| PDP | Average marginal effect | Masks heterogeneity |
| SHAP | Per-observation direction + magnitude | Computationally intensive |

SHAP provides **interpretability** for complex models:
you can show that high-rainfall sites drive high O horizon predictions through a
positive SHAP contribution, confirming pedological plausibility for each mapped area
rather than just on average.

## Setup: Prepare the SHAP Model

```{r shap-setup}
# Install if needed: install.packages(c("fastshap", "shapviz"))
library(fastshap)
library(shapviz)

# ── Ensure the final model exists in environment ──────────────────────────
# (rf_final from Part 10 must be in the environment, trained on Otot)
# If re-running standalone, recreate it here:

soildata_nohist <- droplevels(subset(
  read.csv("soildata.csv"), order != "histosol"
))

predictors <- c(
  "rainfall",   "geology",    "aachn",      "dem10m",     "downslpgra",
  "eastness",   "greenrefl",  "landsatb1",  "landsatb2",  "landsatb3",
  "landsatb7",  "maxc100",    "maxent",     "minc100",    "mirref",
  "ndvi",       "northeastn", "northness",  "northwestn", "planc100",
  "proc100",    "protection", "relpos11",   "slp50",      "solar",
  "tanc75"
)

set.seed(42)
rf_shap <- ranger(
  formula       = Otot ~ .,
  data          = soildata_nohist[, c("Otot", predictors)],
  num.trees     = 500,
  mtry          = dep_tr_bor$bestTune$mtry,
  min.node.size = dep_tr_bor$bestTune$min.node.size,
  splitrule     = dep_tr_bor$bestTune$splitrule,
  importance    = "permutation",
  seed          = 42
)

cat(sprintf("OOB R\u00b2:   %.3f\n", rf_shap$r.squared))
cat(sprintf("OOB RMSE (cm): %.2f\n", sqrt(rf_shap$prediction.error)))
```

## Compute SHAP Values

```{r shap-compute, cache=TRUE}
# ── Prediction wrapper required by fastshap ────────────────────────────────
pfun <- function(object, newdata) {
  predict(object, data = newdata)$predictions
}

# ── Monte Carlo SHAP approximation ─────────────────────────────────────────
# nsim = 100 gives stable estimates; increase to 200 for final analysis
# This takes ~30–60 seconds depending on hardware
set.seed(42)
shap_vals <- fastshap::explain(
  object        = rf_shap,
  X             = soildata_nohist[, predictors],
  pred_wrapper  = pfun,
  nsim          = 100
)

# shap_vals is an nsample × nfeature matrix (cm units)
dim(shap_vals)
head(round(shap_vals[, 1:6], 4))
```

## Global Importance (Mean |SHAP|)

```{r shap-global-importance, fig.height=5}
# Mean absolute SHAP = global variable importance (model-agnostic, unbiased)
mean_abs_shap <- colMeans(abs(shap_vals)) |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |>
  (\(x) data.frame(
    feature        = factor(names(x), levels = rev(names(x))),
    mean_abs_shap  = x
  ))()

ggplot(mean_abs_shap, aes(x = mean_abs_shap, y = feature)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c5f2e", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_abs_shap, 3)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2, color = "gray30") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Mean |SHAP| — Global Variable Importance",
    subtitle = "O Horizon Thickness RF-WV Study Area",
    x        = "Mean absolute SHAP value  (cm units)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10))
```

> **Comparison with permutation importance:** Do the top-ranked SHAP features agree
> with the permutation VIP from Part 9? They typically agree on the top 3–4 but may
> diverge for correlated mid-importance features. SHAP handles collinearity more
> gracefully because it distributes credit across correlated features.

## Beeswarm Plot: Direction and Magnitude

The beeswarm (SHAP summary) plot simultaneously shows importance (x-axis spread),
direction (positive = increases prediction), and feature value (colour) for every
observation. This is the single most informative diagnostic plot in an interpretable
ML workflow.

```{r shap-beeswarm, fig.height=7, fig.width=9}
# Build long-format data frame for ggplot beeswarm
X_mat <- as.data.frame(soildata_nohist[, predictors])

# Normalise each feature to [0, 1] for colour mapping
numeric_cols <- names(X_mat)[sapply(X_mat, is.numeric)]

X_norm <- as.data.frame(lapply(X_mat[, numeric_cols, drop = FALSE], function(v) {
  rng <- range(v, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (diff(rng) == 0) return(rep(0.5, length(v)))
  (v - rng[1]) / diff(rng)
}))

# Add geology back as numeric (integer codes) so join has no NULLs
X_norm_full <- X_norm
if ("geology" %in% colnames(X_mat)) {
  X_norm_full$geology <- as.numeric(as.factor(X_mat$geology))
  # re-normalise to 0-1
  rng <- range(X_norm_full$geology, na.rm = TRUE)
  X_norm_full$geology <- (X_norm_full$geology - rng[1]) / diff(rng)
}

# Rebuild shap_long with X_norm_full
shap_long <- as.data.frame(shap_vals) |>
  tibble::rowid_to_column("obs") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-obs, names_to = "feature", values_to = "shap") |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    X_norm_full |>
      tibble::rowid_to_column("obs") |>
      tidyr::pivot_longer(-obs, names_to = "feature", values_to = "feat_norm") |>
      dplyr::mutate(feat_norm = as.numeric(feat_norm)),
    by = c("obs", "feature")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    feat_norm = as.numeric(feat_norm),
    feature   = factor(feature,
                       levels = rev(levels(mean_abs_shap$feature)))
  )

# Verify
str(shap_long$feat_norm)
sum(is.na(shap_long$feat_norm))

ggplot(shap_long, aes(x = shap, y = feature, colour = feat_norm)) +
  ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(
    groupOnX    = FALSE,
    size        = 1.2,
    alpha       = 0.55,
    cex         = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    low      = "#1565C0",
    mid      = "#E0E0E0",
    high     = "#B71C1C",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    name     = "Feature value\n(normalised)\nLow ← → High"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = "SHAP Beeswarm — Direction & Magnitude",
    subtitle = "Each dot = one observation  |  Colour = feature value",
    x        = "SHAP value  (impact on O horizon prediction, cm)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

> **How to read this plot:**
> 
> - **Horizontal position** = how much this feature pushed the prediction up (right)
>   or down (left) for each observation.
> - **Colour** = the feature's actual value for that observation (red = high, blue = low).
> - **Width of the cloud** = overall importance of the feature (same ranking as Mean |SHAP|).
> - **Pedological check:** For a well-specified DSM model you expect:
>   - `maxent` red dots on the right (high terrain complexity → topographically protected positions → thick O horizons)
>   - `solar` red dots on the left (high solar = warm dry sites → thin O horizons)
>   - `northwestn` / `northness` red dots on the right (cool NW-facing aspects → reduced insolation, slower decomposition → thicker O)

## SHAP Dependence Plots

A SHAP dependence plot shows one feature's SHAP values against its actual values.
The colour encodes a second feature, revealing interaction effects.

```{r shap-dependence, fig.height=8, fig.width=10}
# Get top 2 features by mean |SHAP| for the plot
top2 <- as.character(mean_abs_shap$feature[1:2])
f1   <- top2[1]
f2   <- top2[2]

# Build dependence data: feature 1 SHAP vs feature 1 value, colored by feature 2
dep_df <- data.frame(
  x_val   = X_mat[[f1]],
  shap_f1 = shap_vals[, f1],    # matrix column indexing
  col_var = X_mat[[f2]]
)

p_dep1 <- ggplot(dep_df, aes(x = x_val, y = shap_f1, colour = col_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
              colour = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = f2, option = "D") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(
    title    = paste("SHAP Dependence:", f1),
    subtitle = paste("Color =", f2, "  (interaction signal)"),
    x        = f1,
    y        = paste("SHAP value for", f1)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Second dependence plot: feature 2
dep_df2 <- data.frame(
  x_val   = X_mat[[f2]],
  shap_f2 = shap_vals[, f2],    # matrix column indexing
  col_var = X_mat[[f1]]
)

p_dep2 <- ggplot(dep_df2, aes(x = x_val, y = shap_f2, colour = col_var)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
              colour = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = f1, option = "C") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(
    title    = paste("SHAP Dependence:", f2),
    subtitle = paste("Color =", f1, "  (interaction signal)"),
    x        = f2,
    y        = paste("SHAP value for", f2)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_dep1, p_dep2, ncol = 2)
```

> **Interaction signal:** If the colours in a dependence plot form a gradient pattern
> (e.g., red points cluster in the upper-right), the effect of feature 1 on the
> prediction *depends on* the value of feature 2 — a true interaction. This is
> information PDPs cannot show because they average across that heterogeneity.

**Interpretation:**
The left panel shows northwestn has a clean, independent effect on O horizon thickness — SHAP values rise monotonically from −0.5 cm (SE-facing) to +1.0 cm (NW-facing) with no colour gradient, confirming aspect operates additively regardless of terrain complexity. The right panel reveals a one-directional interaction: maxent's contribution to O horizon thickness is amplified on NW-facing slopes (yellow dots consistently above the smooth) but suppressed on SE-facing slopes (purple dots below). The bottom-left cluster of yellow dots at low maxent confirms that NW aspect alone — without topographic complexity — adds little through the maxent pathway. Together the panels describe a coherent soil-landscape mechanism: cool NW-facing aspects and dissected terrain independently favour organic matter accumulation, but their combination produces the thickest O horizons in the dataset.


## Waterfall Plot: Explaining One Prediction

Waterfall plots decompose a single prediction into its SHAP contributions —
useful for explaining to a field scientist *why* the model predicted a particular
value at a specific pedon location.

```{r shap-waterfall, fig.height=6}
# ── Use shapviz for polished single-observation plots ──────────────────────
sv <- shapviz(
  object = shap_vals,          # matrix of SHAP values
  X      = X_mat               # original feature values (for display)
)

# Find the observation with the highest predicted O horizon (most interesting)
best_obs  <- which.max(rf_shap$predictions)
worst_obs <- which.min(rf_shap$predictions)

# Waterfall for the thickest predicted O horizon
sv_waterfall(sv, row_id = best_obs, max_display = 12) +
  labs(title = paste0("SHAP Waterfall — Obs ", best_obs,
                      " (highest predicted O thickness)"),
       subtitle = paste0("Predicted Otot: ",
                         round(rf_shap$predictions[best_obs], 1),
                         " cm"))
```

```{r shap-waterfall2, fig.height=6}
# Waterfall for the thinnest predicted O horizon
sv_waterfall(sv, row_id = worst_obs, max_display = 12) +
  labs(title = paste0("SHAP Waterfall — Obs ", worst_obs,
                      " (lowest predicted O thickness)"),
       subtitle = paste0("Predicted Otot: ",
                         round(rf_shap$predictions[worst_obs], 1),
                         " cm"))
```

> **Questions:**
> 1. Do the top SHAP features (Mean |SHAP| bar chart) align with your pedological
>    expectations for O horizon development in West Virginia?
> 2. In the beeswarm plot, identify one feature where blue dots (low values) fall to
>    the right. What does this tell you about the direction of that feature's effect?
> 3. Compare the waterfall for the thickest vs. thinnest predicted site. Which features
>    *switch direction* between the two observations, suggesting site-specific interactions?
> 4. Express the SHAP value for the top feature at the thickest-predicted site as a
>    percentage increase in predicted O thickness (hint: exp(SHAP) − 1).

# Part 10 — Quantile Regression Forest and Uncertainty

## Theory: Beyond Point Predictions

A standard RF predicts the **conditional mean** $E[Y | X = x]$. In DSM this is
insufficient for operational decision-making — field staff need to know not just
the predicted value but **how confident** the model is at each location.

**Quantile Regression Forest (QRF, Meinshausen 2006)** extends RF to predict the
full conditional distribution $F(Y | X = x)$ by retaining all training observations
in each terminal leaf rather than only the leaf mean. Any quantile can then be
read from this empirical distribution:

$$\hat{Q}_\tau(Y | X = x) = \text{weighted quantile of training responses in leaf}$$

This enables **prediction intervals** without distributional assumptions — no need to
assume normality:

- **Median** ($\tau = 0.5$): robust point prediction
- **90% PI**: $[\hat{Q}_{0.05},\ \hat{Q}_{0.95}]$
- **PI width**: a spatial uncertainty map — wide intervals flag sites for targeted field verification


## Fit QRF

```{r qrf-fit}
# ── QRF requires the quantregForest package ────────────────────────────────
# install.packages("quantregForest")
library(quantregForest)

# ── Prepare training and validation matrices ───────────────────────────────
# Convert factors to numeric in both sets
prep_qrf <- function(df, predictors) {
  df[, predictors] <- lapply(df[, predictors], function(v) {
    if (is.numeric(v)) v else as.numeric(as.factor(v))
  })
  as.matrix(df[, predictors])
}

x_train <- prep_qrf(cal_nohist, predictors)
y_train <- cal_nohist$Otot

x_val   <- prep_qrf(val, predictors)
y_val   <- val$Otot

# ── Fit QRF on training data only ─────────────────────────────────────────
set.seed(42)
qrf_model <- quantregForest(
  x        = x_train,
  y        = y_train,
  ntree    = 500,
  mtry     = max(2, floor(length(predictors) / 3)),
  nodesize = 5
)

# ── Predict on held-out validation set ────────────────────────────────────
qrf_pred_cm <- predict(qrf_model, newdata = x_val, what = 0.50)
qrf_lo_cm   <- pmax(predict(qrf_model, newdata = x_val, what = 0.05), 0)
qrf_hi_cm   <- predict(qrf_model, newdata = x_val, what = 0.95)
qrf_width   <- qrf_hi_cm - qrf_lo_cm

# ── Honest PICP on validation set ─────────────────────────────────────────
inside <- y_val >= qrf_lo_cm & y_val <= qrf_hi_cm
picp   <- mean(inside)

cat(sprintf("Validation n:                 %d\n",   length(y_val)))
cat(sprintf("Median predicted O thickness: %.2f cm\n", median(qrf_pred_cm)))
cat(sprintf("Median 90%% PI width:          %.2f cm\n", median(qrf_width)))
cat(sprintf("Min / Max PI width:           %.2f / %.2f cm\n", min(qrf_width), max(qrf_width)))
cat(sprintf("90%% PI coverage (PICP):       %.3f  (target: 0.90)\n", picp))
cat(sprintf("Calibration:                  %s\n",
            ifelse(picp > 0.92, "conservative (too wide)",
            ifelse(picp < 0.88, "anti-conservative (too narrow)",
                               "well-calibrated"))))

```

## Prediction Interval Calibration

**Calibration** checks whether stated 90% PIs actually contain the observation 90% of the time
(PICP — Prediction Interval Coverage Probability). Uncalibrated intervals are misleading
regardless of model accuracy.

```{r qrf-calibration}
# ── PICP: fraction of observations inside the PI ──────────────────────────
inside <- y_val >= qrf_lo_cm &
          y_val <= qrf_hi_cm

picp <- mean(inside)
cat(sprintf("90%% PI coverage (PICP): %.3f  (target: 0.90)\n", picp))
cat(sprintf("Overcoverage (>0.90 = conservative): %s\n",
            ifelse(picp > 0.90, "YES", "NO")))
```

> **Important:** This PICP is computed on **training data** and will be optimistic
> (similar to OOB error). For a proper calibration assessment use held-out test data
> or spatial CV predictions. A PICP > 0.90 means intervals are conservative (too wide);
> PICP < 0.90 means they are anti-conservative (too narrow, over-confident).

## Visualise Intervals

```{r qrf-interval-plot, fig.height=5}
# Sort by predicted value for a clean ribbon plot
plot_df <- data.frame(
  obs    = y_val,          # was soildata_qrf$Otot
  pred   = qrf_pred_cm,
  lo     = qrf_lo_cm,
  hi     = qrf_hi_cm,
  width  = qrf_width,
  inside = inside
) |> dplyr::arrange(pred)

plot_df$rank <- seq_len(nrow(plot_df))

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = rank)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#a8d5a2", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), colour = "#2c5f2e", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = obs, colour = inside), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("TRUE"  = "#333333",
               "FALSE" = "#e07b54"),
    labels = c("TRUE"  = "Inside PI",
               "FALSE" = "Outside PI"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "QRF 90% Prediction Intervals — O Horizon Thickness",
    subtitle = paste0("Sorted by predicted value  |  PICP = ",
                      round(picp, 3), "  |  Orange = outside PI"),
    x        = "Observation rank (sorted by prediction)",
    y        = "O Horizon Thickness (cm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
QRF 90% prediction intervals evaluated on a held-out validation set (n ≈ 75) achieved a PICP of 0.918, indicating well-calibrated slightly conservative intervals. Median PI width was 5.00 cm. Interval width scaled appropriately with predicted O horizon thickness, reflecting greater model uncertainty at thick O horizon sites underrepresented in training data.


## PI Width as Uncertainty Map

PI width is heterogeneous across the landscape — some sites are modelled confidently
and others are not. Mapping PI width alongside the point prediction is important for communicating spatial uncertainty.

```{r qrf-uncertainty-map, fig.height=5}
# ── Attach uncertainty to validation spatial data frame ───────────────────
val_sf_qrf <- st_as_sf(
  cbind(
    val,
    qrf_pred_cm = as.numeric(qrf_pred_cm),
    qrf_lo_cm   = as.numeric(qrf_lo_cm),
    qrf_hi_cm   = as.numeric(qrf_hi_cm),
    qrf_width   = as.numeric(qrf_width)
  ),
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  crs    = 4326
)

# ── Static map: PI width as bubble size + color ───────────────────────────
ggplot(val_sf_qrf) +
  geom_sf(aes(colour = qrf_width, size = qrf_width), alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(
    name   = "PI Width (cm)",
    option = "plasma",
    trans  = "sqrt",
    guide  = guide_legend()
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    name   = "PI Width (cm)",      # same name merges the two legends into one
    range  = c(0.5, 5),
    trans  = "sqrt"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "QRF 90% Prediction Interval Width",
    subtitle = "Validation set  |  Large / bright = high uncertainty; small / dark = high confidence"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "right",
    plot.title       = element_text(size = 13),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

Interpretation: PI width typically increases with predicted value for right-skewed soil properties — the model is less certain about thick O horizons (rare observations) than thin ones (abundant observations). This is the correct behavior and reflects training data density, not a model flaw. The spatial map shows uncertainty is not randomly distributed across the landscape — high-uncertainty sites (wide PI, large bright yellow/orange symbols) cluster in the southern portion of the transect around 38.60–38.65°N.

```{r qrf-width-vs-pred, fig.height=4}
# PI width vs predicted value: does uncertainty scale with magnitude?
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = pred, y = width)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#5b9bd5", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", colour = "#e07b54", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "PI Width vs Predicted O Thickness",
    x     = "QRF Predicted Median (cm)",
    y     = "90% PI Width (cm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Interpretation:*** PI width shows a U-shaped relationship with predicted O thickness rather than a simple monotonic increase. The model is most confident at moderate predicted values (3–5 cm) where training observations are most dense. Uncertainty is elevated at both extremes — at very low predicted values (0–3 cm) intervals remain wide (~12–15 cm) because near-zero O horizon sites are environmentally ambiguous and difficult to distinguish from thin-but-present O horizons using the available covariates. At high predicted values (>8 cm) PI width rises to ~20 cm and plateaus, reflecting the scarcity of thick O horizon observations in the training data.

> 2. Which observations (if any) fall outside the PI? Do they share any characteristics
